_what: What the simulated floor at ACME bottling does that no PLC reports: which scale takes a fill-weight reading, how far the drifting one is out, which stops it labels from the plant's own vocabulary, and how the shift supervisor dispositions a non-conformance. Read only by `fsmes run-operations`.
_why_data: The same argument as line.json. A story scripted in a loop body cannot be read by a test, by a scorer, or by the person who has to explain the records afterwards - so the stories this floor plants are written here, each with the trace it leaves, and `fsmes.sim.operations` never changes when the story does.
_the_stories_planted_here: the drifting gauge: SCALE-FILL-02 reads high by 0.01 g for every day since its last calibration, up to 0.6 g, and is clean again the shift the supervisor calibrates it. Trace: group the fill-weight checks by gauge and SCALE-FILL-02's mean sits above SCALE-FILL-01's.

the night shift: two readings of one bottle disagree by more at night than by day, because the plant at night is thinner - fewer people, less light, nobody to ask. Trace: the spread of the night shift's readings is wider than the day's, while the process behind them is the same.

the stops: this floor labels what it sees stopped from the six approved reasons, and leaves the ones it genuinely cannot explain as `not_yet_determined` rather than guessing. Trace: the downtime pareto has bars with names on them, and says how much came from the list.

the nozzle the changeover left behind: for twenty-five line minutes after each changeover the fill-height sample means sit about a millimetre and a half high - 2.9 sigma of a sample mean - while the sample ranges stay where they were. Trace: on the fill_height chart the means after a labelled changeover stop are above centre, nearly all of them past the two-sigma line, and the range chart beside them is flat.

the cold product, which is the line's story and this file's trace: for half an hour (7:00-7:30 of the shift in line.json) the cola reaching the filler is two degrees cold, so the bottles fill light and the fill-height sample means this file computes sit about a millimetre and a half LOW - the mirror of the changeover story above. Trace: the X-bar chart walks below its lower two-sigma line for two or three samples while the range chart stays flat, and the sample's own panel shows FILL01.ProductTemp down at 6.4 degC in the station's tags block.

the maintenance order nobody starts: the filler's chiller condenser clean (PM-FILL-CHILLER) has never been serviced, so the supervisor raises it in the first minutes of the shift and then runs to the end of the order - the job sits at `due` in the backlog for eight hours. Trace: one preventive order on FILL01 on the Maintenance page, raised early, never started, with no `maintenance.started` audit row; and a chiller outlet temperature on the same machine that climbs all afternoon because of it. Link 2 of the chain in line.json.

the paperwork: the supervisor reviews a non-conformance, decides what happens to the material, and closes it - and leaves a few open on purpose, because a plant where every finding is closed by the end of the shift is not a plant.
_see_also: The line's own stories - the nozzle-pressure dip, the first fills after a changeover, the tag that goes quiet, the washer running hot, and the product running cold - are in this pack's `line.json`, because they are things the machines do. This file is only what the people do. `labs/kepsim/line.json` is the same line as one hour, kept as the reference CI replays.

planning._what: How many orders the simulated production planner keeps in this plant's book, ahead of the line.
planning._why: Because a lab plant has no ERP and nobody else was going to. The pack seeds ten orders - about twenty-five hours of line time - and this plant runs for weeks: on 2026-10-07 at 04:21 UTC, forty-three hours after it was built, bottling finished `WO-ACME-4720` and from then on measured fill weight, fill height and everything else into no order at all. The station page said *Nothing queued on this machine*, the characteristic dropdown was empty, and every quality check carried no order. That is not the plant being honest about an empty book, it is the plant having nobody to fill one. In a real plant orders come from a planner or from an ERP, never from the floor; this names the planner.
planning._keep_planned: Three planned orders behind whatever is on the line, which on this book of 12,000-19,200 bottles is somewhere between eight and twelve hours of work in hand - about what a bottling line's schedule looks like on a Monday morning. `FLOOR-PLAN` creates them over `POST /workorders`, copying material, quantity and priority from this plant's own book in rotation and continuing its code sequence from `WO-ACME-4720`. It never releases one: the simulated shift supervisor still does that, so the audit trail reads planner, then supervisor, then floor. Zero - the default, and what every pack that leaves this block out gets - means no planner, the book empties when the pack's orders are done, and the floor says so once.

measurement._what: How a number on a tag becomes a measurement somebody took.
measurement._stale_after_s: A process value older than this is not a reading. The floor records a plausible value instead, with no gauge and no station, and says so in the log - which is what a shift does when the display is frozen and nobody has climbed up to look. Seconds on the clock, not line seconds: how often a sample arrives is a fact about this MES (`opc_min_history_ms`, five seconds as shipped) rather than about the line, so sixty is twelve samples' worth of silence at any replay speed. It does mean a replay fast enough to run the fifteen-minute quiet window in under a minute never trips it - at 30x that window is thirty seconds of real time - which is a property of replaying an hour in a minute and not of the rule.

fill_height._spread: Millimetres. How much two readings of the same bottle disagree on the bench gauge, day shift. The gauge resolves to a tenth of a millimetre, so this is where the operator rests the bottle rather than the instrument.

gauges._share: One bench gauge at the QI station. Every reading in every sample is taken with it, which is what makes the five readings of a sample comparable with each other.

fill_weight._spread: Grams. How much two readings of the same bottle disagree, day shift. The scales resolve to a tenth of a gram, so this is the hand and the bottle rather than the instrument.

gauges._share: The scale that lives at the filler takes three readings in four.

gauges._drift: Grams per day since its last calibration, to a ceiling of 0.6 g. A real gauge does not drift forever: it goes out, stays out, and is found at the next calibration. The pack has this one calibrated 84 days ago against a 90-day interval, so it is reading about 0.6 g high today and is due this week.

sampling._what: How this floor gets the pieces for a sample, for a characteristic no machine on the line publishes a tag for. Fill height is measured by hand on a bench: five bottles come off the filler, are carried to the QI station and are measured one after another, and the five readings are posted together as one sample.
sampling._why_data: Because the arithmetic that turns a weight into a height is this plant's, not the product's. A different bottle has a different formula and nothing in `fsmes.sim` should know either.

fill_height._every_line_s: Line seconds between samples: every fifteen minutes of line time, which is four samples an hour. Divided by the replay speed like every other cadence on this floor.
fill_height._from: The five pieces are the last five *stored* FillWeight samples off the filler - five different bottles, each weighed at a different instant, which is what a sample of five is. If five distinct readings newer than the last sample are not there, this floor takes nothing and says so once rather than measuring the same bottle five times.
fill_height._convert: height_mm = 12.0 + 0.26 x fill_weight_g. One straight line, because the bottle is a cylinder over the band that matters: 500 g of cola stands 142 mm up the glass, and a gram either way is a quarter of a millimetre. The neck and the base are not in this band and are not modelled.
fill_height._piece_to_piece: Millimetres, one sigma. The glass itself: two bottles holding the same weight do not stand at the same height, because the moulding varies. This is the bottle-to-bottle variation a sample of five is taken to measure, and it is deliberately larger than the gauge's own spread - an X-bar and R chart whose range came mostly from the instrument would be charting the instrument.
fill_height._after_changeover: The planted cause. For twenty-five minutes of line time after each changeover the heights sit a millimetre and a half high: the nozzle setting the changeover left behind fills a shade over, which the checkweigher's own band absorbs and the height chart does not.
fill_height._how_big_a_millimetre_and_a_half_is: Measured off this plant's own chart, forty-five samples of five - 225 readings: R-bar is 2.69 mm, so the within-sample sigma is R-bar / d2 = 2.69 / 2.326 = 1.16 mm, a sample mean's own sigma is 1.16 / sqrt(5) = 0.52 mm, and the X-bar limits are X-doublebar +/- A2 x R-bar = 141.88 +/- 0.577 x 2.69 = 141.88 +/- 1.55 mm, which is 140.33 to 143.43. So 1.5 mm is 2.9 sigma of a sample mean, 1.3 times the whole within-sample sigma, and more than four times the glass's own `piece_to_piece` 0.35. It lands just under A2 x R-bar, and that is the useful part: the two-sigma line at 142.91 is broken by nearly every post-changeover sample and the three-sigma line at 143.43 by only the highest, so rule 2 - two of three beyond two sigma - is what fires reliably, and rule 1 catches the tall ones. On the hour this was measured 7 of 9 post-changeover sample means sat above the two-sigma line and 0 of 15 settled ones did, and rule 1 fired once early in the run while the limits were still narrow (they widen as post-changeover samples join the chart, which is worth knowing: a shift that lives on the chart partly hides itself). Single bottles stay in spec: the arithmetic puts a reading past the 145 mm upper spec at a few percent, and none of those 45 post-changeover readings crossed it - the highest was 144.5.
fill_height._why_not_half_a_millimetre: It was 0.5 mm until 2026-10-07, which on the same chart is 1.0 sigma of a sample mean and sits nearly three sigma inside the upper control limit: a shift a reader could find by splitting the means on the changeover, but one that effectively never fired a control rule where anybody was watching. It was raised on 2026-10-07 by somebody who wanted to watch a rule fire on fill height and could not. 1.5 mm is the smallest shift that fires inside an hour and still leaves the sample ranges alone and single bottles in spec - which is the whole point of the story: the process moved, its spread did not.
fill_height._trace: The sample means after a labelled `changeover` stop sit above the centre line, nearly all of them past the two-sigma line and the tallest past the upper control limit, and the range chart beside them shows no signal at all - every one of its points is inside its own upper limit. The process moved, the spread did not, which is exactly what an X-bar chart is for and what an individuals chart on fill weight never showed.
fill_height._why_not_two_hours: The handoff asked for about two hours. When this was written the plant replayed the reference hour, which changes over inside its own loop, so a two-hour window would never close and every sample on the chart would be a post-changeover one - the planted cause would have been the whole chart and visible as nothing. Since 2026-10-08 the plant replays an eight-hour shift (line.json beside this file) with one changeover in it, so that particular trap is gone; twenty-five line minutes stays, because it is still between one and two samples' worth after the changeover and that is a step a reader can see against the settled samples either side of it. A longer window now would only make the step harder to date.

maintenance._what: What the simulated shift supervisor does with this plant's maintenance backlog.
maintenance._why_data: The same argument as everything else in this file. Whether a floor raises its own due work is a fact about how a plant is run - some plants raise it from a planner's nightly sweep, some from the shift that finds it - and a plant that raised it from a loop body in `fsmes.sim.operations` could not be read by a test or turned off by a pack.
maintenance._raise_due: The shift supervisor calls `POST /maintenance/raise` on his own pass, which raises one preventive order for every plan this plant says has come due and nothing for the plans that have not. Idempotent in the product, so a supervisor who looks every few minutes does not bury the floor in duplicates. `FLOOR-SUP` and not `FLOOR-SIM`: raising work is a supervisor's act and the audit row has to say so. False - the default, and what every pack that leaves this block out gets - means nobody raises anything and the Maintenance page shows plans coming due with no orders against them, which is a real plant with no planner and not an interesting one.
maintenance._dispatch: The same supervisor, on the same pass, calls `POST /maintenance/dispatch` after raising - and the order matters: work nobody has been given is the state an order spends its first seconds in, not its shift. The product's own rules decide who gets what (`dispatch_rules.json` in this pack's masterdata: safety first, filler electrical work to the nearest electrician, the rest spread by turns), and each assignment leaves an audit row naming the rule that made it. Idempotent, like raising, so a supervisor who looks every twenty seconds hands nothing out twice. False - the default, and what every pack written before the maintenance crew existed gets - means the work is raised and sits with nobody's name on it, which is a real plant that has not written its rules down.
maintenance._crew: The crew does the work it was given. On each pass, for every person on this shift's roster holding an `assigned` order, the floor asks the two questions a mechanic asks: is my window open, and can I get at the machine. The window is the order's own (`anytime` always; `between_orders` only when no order is on the line; `end_of_shift` only inside the last `expected_minutes` of the shift). Getting at the machine means `needs_stop` is false, or the machine has been standing for `standing_s` - stopped, rather than momentarily quiet. Both true: he walks over (`walk_s`), starts it, and when the job's time is up completes it with what he found, how long the machine was down and his own name on it. One person, one job at a time - the product's dispatcher already refuses a busy person a second. He never stops a machine that is making something, never finishes an order he did not watch start, and never invents a reason for a job that waits: the jobs that wait say why in the log, once each. False, and the default, is every pack written before 2026-10-09: the work is raised, handed out, and waits. Those packs score exactly as they did.
maintenance._walk_s: How long it takes to get to the machine with the tools after being given the job, in line seconds. Without it an order is assigned and started in the same second, and the Maintenance page shows a plant where nobody walks anywhere - which reads as a simulation rather than a shift. Three minutes is the bottling line end to end plus the stores. It is line time, so a replay at 30x waits six real seconds.
maintenance._standing_s: How long a machine has to have been standing, in line seconds, before a job that needs it stopped may be started on it. Ten minutes. Without it this floor reads every pause as its chance: the four-minute changeover at 16800 s, a starved palletiser between micro stops, the twelve seconds the loader is down at 4200 s. A mechanic who took the filler apart in a four-minute changeover would be the reason the line could not restart, and the stop he booked would land inside a scripted planned stop and be scored as a changeover called downtime - which is the one availability defect `fsmes score` exists to catch. So the rule is the plant's rule rather than a number tuned for the scorer: a machine that has just gone quiet is starved, not stopped, and a job that needs the line stopped waits for the line to be stopped.
maintenance._stop_reason: Which of this plant's approved downtime reasons a stop for maintenance is booked under (`downtime_reasons.json` in this pack's masterdata). The sentence the crew writes beside it carries the order's code - `planned maintenance PM-...` - so the stop and the job are one event in the records rather than two a reader has to join by eye. It is a code and not a typed sentence because this plant has an approved vocabulary and the product refuses a stop that is not labelled from it; a pack with no vocabulary can leave this out and the crew sends the sentence alone, as it always could.

PM-PAL-GREASE: All eight points taken grease, arm movement free.
Greased; number three nipple weeping slightly, watch it next week.
PM-LD-BELT: Belt within tension spec, no edge wear.
Tension low by 4 N, adjusted on the tensioner.
PM-RD-BEARING: Play within limits on both shafts.
Lower shaft at the limit of play; recommend a bearing at the next stop.
PM-FILL-SEALS: Six valve seals replaced, two were hardened.
All twelve seals replaced, filler run up and leak-checked clean.
PM-FILL-CHILLER: Condenser 40% blocked, cleaned; outlet temperature 8.4 to 6.1 C.
Coil washed, fan bearing noisy, refrigerant pressures normal.
PM-WASH-NOZZLE: Nozzles descaled, manifold flushed, spray pattern even.
Four nozzles replaced rather than descaled, scale too far gone.

maintenance._findings: What the mechanic writes in the box, one list per plan, picked from the plan's own list by the run's seeded random stream. It is here and not in masterdata because this floor reads the plant only through the HTTP API, exactly as a browser does, and a note on a masterdata row never reaches the database - the `_why_needs_stop` sentences beside the plans do explain themselves there, which is where somebody editing a plan will look. A plan with no list here is completed with no findings, which is honest: a job somebody did and wrote nothing about.
maintenance._expected_done: Which orders this shift is meant to get through, written down so a reader can tell a broken replay from a true one. It drives nothing: the floor starts whatever the windows and the machine states allow, and this is the answer key for the two that should come out `done` with findings, a measured downtime of nought and a mechanic's name on them. The palletiser grease (seven-day calendar, never serviced) and the denester bearing play (fortnightly, never done) are both due in the first pass and neither needs the machine stopped, so both are greased and felt while the line runs - which is the ordinary half of maintenance and the half a plant does not notice. Two and not three: the four jobs that are left are a longer story, and `_what_waits_and_why` is it.
maintenance._what_waits_and_why: Three of the six, each for its own reason, and none of them a mechanic ignoring his list. PM-FILL-CHILLER: ninety minutes with the filler isolated, window `between_orders`, and this plant releases the next order as the last one finishes, so the gap never comes - raised in the first minutes, given to an electrician by the FILL-ELEC rule in the same pass, still `assigned` with no `maintenance.started` audit row at the end of the shift. That is link 2 of the chain in line.json, and it is now a recorded reason rather than an absence. PM-FILL-SEALS: `anytime`, so its window is never the problem - but it needs the filler stopped, and the longest the filler stands still on this shift is the four-minute changeover, against a forty-five-minute job and a ten-minute `standing_s`. It waits for a stop that does not come. PM-WASH-NOZZLE: its window is the last hour of the shift, read on the plant's own clock, and a replay that plays eight hours in sixteen minutes never reaches its own last hour - so on the lab plant, which runs at its own speed, the descale goes in at the end of the day, and on a replay it honestly waits. Three jobs, three different fields, three sentences a supervisor can act on. The point of the two columns is exactly this: the Maintenance page can tell them apart.
maintenance._what_else_lands_in_the_backlog: More than the chain's one order, on purpose, and how much more depends on how fast the plant is played. The two calendar plans (PM-FILL-CHILLER, 30 days, and PM-PAL-GREASE, 7 days) and the fortnightly PM-RD-BEARING have never been done on a fresh plant, so all three come due in the first pass; PM-WASH-NOZZLE is produced_qty and comes due when the washer has made its twenty thousand, which it does part way through any eight-hour shift. The two runtime plans (PM-FILL-SEALS at four running hours, PM-LD-BELT at six) come due on the lab plant, which runs for days, and do NOT come due on a 30x replay - running hours are real hours counted from the machine's own state history, and sixteen real minutes is sixteen minutes of them however many shift hours they stand for. Nothing here inflates them, which is why the replay's backlog is four orders and the lab's is six. A backlog with one item in it is a backlog nobody had to search, so the chain's answer key names its link by PLAN code (`PM-FILL-CHILLER`) rather than by 'the overdue order'.
maintenance._when: `overdue` raises only what is genuinely due; `due_soon` would also raise what this plant's own warning fraction has flagged. Overdue is what the product's own `POST /maintenance/raise` does and the only value this floor implements today - it is written down so a pack can see which of the two it is getting rather than having to read the source.
maintenance._was_why_nobody_starts_it: Kept, because it was true until 2026-10-09 and the chain's second link was built on it: There is deliberately no key here that starts or completes an order, and no step in `fsmes.sim.operations` that could: this shift gives its work out and runs to the end of the order. That is the honest version of the commonest thing in a bottling plant - the job that is due during a run, is handed to somebody, and waits for the gap between orders - and it is link 2 of the chain in line.json. It matters that it is an ABSENCE rather than a flag: this product has no `deferred` status, so an order sitting at `assigned` all shift with no `maintenance.started` audit row beside it is the only true record of nobody having gone, and inventing a deferral the Maintenance page cannot show would have made the chain unreadable on the screen it is meant to be read on. What the records therefore say, exactly: PM-FILL-CHILLER raised in the first minutes, given to an electrician by the FILL-ELEC rule in the same pass, still `assigned` eight hours later, never started. Until 2026-10-09 it said `due` with nobody's name on it, because this plant had no crew to give it to. If a future floor learns to perform maintenance, the knob goes here beside `raise_due` and `dispatch`, and this note says what changed.

calibration._what: When the simulated shift supervisor calibrates a gauge this floor measures with.
calibration._when: Not `due_soon`. A floor that calibrated on the warning would calibrate the drifting scale in the first twenty seconds of every plant ever built from this pack, and the drifting-gauge story would be over before anybody could open the screen. Overdue is also what a plant with a fortnight's warning window actually does: the warning is for planning the visit, and the visit happens when it falls due. The pack has SCALE-FILL-02 six days from due, so a plant left up for a week sees the whole story - the drift, the calibration, and clean readings after it.

stops._what: Which of this plant's six approved words the floor puts on a stop it watched. Nothing here invents an interval: the MES watched the stop, and this names it afterwards - which is the only moment anybody can, because the moment a machine goes down is the moment nobody knows why yet.
stops._what_it_will_not_say: An idle machine is left unlabelled on purpose. This line's tag map maps starved (2) and blocked (3) both onto `idle`, so by the time the MES holds the interval the difference is gone, and the vocabulary's own `starved` and `blocked` cannot be chosen between from anything that was recorded. Guessing one would put a cause in the pareto that nothing observed. The floor says so once, in its log, as a finding about the state map.
stops._and_the_flickers_are_not_this_file_s_to: Until 2026-10-08 that residue was mostly noise rather than downtime: the generator published every one-second block a full buffer produced, so the reference hour left 124 unlabelled idle intervals across six machines, most of them one to seventeen seconds long, and a quiet sample's panel listed 25 other stops around it. Naming those `micro_stop` here would have been the wrong fix twice over - nobody cleared them, and this file would have been inventing a cause for an artefact of a one-second tick. They are gone at the source instead (`state_filter_s` in line.json), which is where a machine's state filter lives on a real line. What is left unlabelled on this plant is the genuine article: the two-and-a-half-minute starves and blocks the RD breakdown ripples through the buffers, and the loader's 12-second jam. The palletiser's own micro-stops stay unlabelled too, and that is also right: the line publishes them as STOPPED (0), which this plant's tag map folds onto `idle` along with starved and blocked, so by the time the MES holds one there is nothing in the record that says which of the three it was. They are short waits at the line's slowest machine and they belong in performance, not availability - mapping 0 onto `down` to get them named would book about fifty line minutes a shift against availability and turn the OEE lesson this line is built to teach upside down. Measured on the shift of 2026-10-08: 238 of them, 0.5 to 10 wall seconds each, against five unlabelled idles on all the other machines put together.
stops._what_it_misses: A stop shorter than one look (MES_OPS_WATCH_EVERY, 15 s) is never seen and stays unlabelled - the loader's 12-second jam, once a shift. That residue is real and the pareto reports it as unlabelled, which is house rule 3 doing its job rather than a gap in this file.
stops._micro_stop: A stop this short was cleared by whoever was standing there - a jam, a misfeed, a reset. Nothing is broken and nothing needs reporting.
stops._longer_than_a_micro_stop: Longer than a minute and the machine was willing to run, so something failed and somebody fixed it. On this line that is exactly what a `down` state means: the tag map maps only a genuine fault to DOWN.
stops._changeover: A machine in setup on this line is the whole line changing over between orders. Labelling it is what makes it findable later - a planned stop that ended three minutes before a point on the fill-weight chart is the explanation for that point, and an unnamed setup interval explains nothing.

nonconformances._what: What the shift supervisor does with a finding, by rule, so the quality screen shows a plant working through its paperwork rather than a list that only grows.
nonconformances._leave_open: How many of the newest findings are left alone every pass. A plant where nothing is open is as unrealistic as one where nothing is ever closed.

major.reason: Out of specification on a critical characteristic; the affected bottles were scrapped at the filler.

minor.reason: Underweight bottles pulled off the line and refilled on the same order.

otherwise.reason: Inside the customer's own limit though outside ours; released as is on the shift supervisor's name.
